claim: RELA is a master regulator of immune and stress responses.
source: The canonical NF-κB transcription factor RELA is a master regulator of immune and stress responses and is upregulated in pancreatic ductal adenocardinoma (PDAC) tumours.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about RELA function.

claim: RELA is upregulated in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) tumours.
source: The canonical NF-κB transcription factor RELA is a master regulator of immune and stress responses and is upregulated in pancreatic ductal adenocardinoma (PDAC) tumours.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: TNFα stimulation induces rapid, sustained, and non-oscillatory nuclear translocation of RELA in PDAC cell lines.
source: Our observations revealed that TNFα stimulation induces rapid, sustained, and non-oscillatory nuclear translocation of RELA.
evidence: This is a primary finding from live single-cell imaging experiments described in the abstract and Results section.

claim: RELA heterogeneity in PDAC cell lines is dependent on F-actin dynamics.
source: Through Bayesian analysis of single-cell datasets with variation in nuclear RELA, we predicted that RELA heterogeneity in PDAC cell lines is dependent on F-actin dynamics.
evidence: This prediction is based on Bayesian modeling analysis of single-cell datasets.

claim: TNFα induces RELA upregulation of the actin regulators NUAK2 and ARHGAP31.
source: RNA-seq analysis identified distinct clusters of RELA-regulated gene expression in PDAC cells, including TNFα-induced RELA upregulation of the actin regulators NUAK2 and ARHGAP31.
evidence: This finding is based on RNA-seq analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of ARHGAP31 and NUAK2 altered TNFα-stimulated nuclear RELA dynamics in PDAC cells.
source: Further, siRNA-mediated depletion of ARHGAP31 and NUAK2 altered TNFα-stimulated nuclear RELA dynamics in PDAC cells, establishing a novel negative feedback loop that regulates RELA activation by TNFα.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: A novel negative feedback loop regulates RELA activation by TNFα through ARHGAP31 and NUAK2.
source: Further, siRNA-mediated depletion of ARHGAP31 and NUAK2 altered TNFα-stimulated nuclear RELA dynamics in PDAC cells, establishing a novel negative feedback loop that regulates RELA activation by TNFα.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the siRNA depletion experimental results.

claim: RELA is central to the canonical NF-κB signalling pathway.
source: The NF-κB transcription factor RELA is an essential mediator of the inflammatory and immune responses in all mammals (Hayden et al., 2006) and is central to the canonical NF-κB signalling pathway (Ghosh et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ghosh et al., 1998.

claim: Inactive RELA is sequestered in the cytoplasm by IκB proteins.
source: Inactive RELA is sequestered in the cytoplasm by IκB proteins and IκB degradation by upstream cues, such as the potent inflammatory cytokine tumour necrosis factor α (TNFα), enables RELA translocation to the nucleus where RELA regulates gene expression (DiDonato et al., 1997; Zandi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to DiDonato et al., 1997 and Zandi et al., 1997.

claim: IκB degradation by TNFα enables RELA translocation to the nucleus.
source: Inactive RELA is sequestered in the cytoplasm by IκB proteins and IκB degradation by upstream cues, such as the potent inflammatory cytokine tumour necrosis factor α (TNFα), enables RELA translocation to the nucleus where RELA regulates gene expression (DiDonato et al., 1997; Zandi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to DiDonato et al., 1997 and Zandi et al., 1997.

claim: RELA oscillates between the nucleus and cytoplasm in response to TNFα.
source: Live imaging experiments of fluorescently labelled RELA and electrophoretic mobility shift assays have shown that RELA oscillates between the nucleus and cytoplasm in response to TNFα (Hoffmann et al., 2002; Nelson et al., 2004; Sung et al., 2009; Tay et al., 2010; Sero et al., 2015; Zambrano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Oscillations are driven by a negative feedback loop between RELA and particular IκB isoforms.
source: Oscillations are driven by a negative feedback loop between RELA and particular IκB isoforms since the genes encoding IκB proteins are RELA transcriptional targets (Brown et al., 1993; Scott et al., 1993; Sun et al., 1993; Hoffmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 1993; Scott et al., 1993; Sun et al., 1993; Hoffmann et al., 2002.

claim: The genes encoding IκB proteins are RELA transcriptional targets.
source: Oscillations are driven by a negative feedback loop between RELA and particular IκB isoforms since the genes encoding IκB proteins are RELA transcriptional targets (Brown et al., 1993; Scott et al., 1993; Sun et al., 1993; Hoffmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 1993; Scott et al., 1993; Sun et al., 1993; Hoffmann et al., 2002.

claim: The pattern of RELA translocation dictates the specificity and timing of RELA target gene expression.
source: The pattern of RELA translocation has been shown to dictate the specificity and timing of RELA target gene expression, including the genes encoding IκBα, IκBε, and the chemokine RANTES (Ashall et al., 2009; Zambrano et al., 2016; Lane et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ashall et al., 2009; Zambrano et al., 2016; Lane et al., 2017.

claim: Cell shape is a regulator of RELA dynamics in breast cancer cell lines.
source: Previously, we showed that cell shape is a regulator of RELA dynamics in breast cancer cell lines and that breast cancer cells with mesenchymal cell shape (protrusive with low cell–cell contacts) have higher RELA nuclear translocation (Sero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sero et al., 2015.

claim: Breast cancer cells with mesenchymal cell shape have higher RELA nuclear translocation.
source: Previously, we showed that cell shape is a regulator of RELA dynamics in breast cancer cell lines and that breast cancer cells with mesenchymal cell shape (protrusive with low cell–cell contacts) have higher RELA nuclear translocation (Sero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sero et al., 2015.

claim: RELA activity, coupled to cell shape, is predictive of breast cancer progression.
source: We also identified that RELA activity, coupled to cell shape, is predictive of breast cancer progression (Sailem and Bakal, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sailem and Bakal, 2017.

claim: Chemically inhibiting actin or tubulin dynamics can increase RELA binding to DNA.
source: Although the mechanistic basis for how cell shape regulates RELA remains poorly understood, studies have shown that chemically inhibiting actin or tubulin dynamics can increase RELA binding to DNA and RELA-dependent gene expression (Rosette and Karin, 1995; Bourgarel-Rey et al., 2001; Németh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rosette and Karin, 1995; Bourgarel-Rey et al., 2001; Németh et al., 2004.

claim: Chemically inhibiting actin or tubulin dynamics can increase RELA-dependent gene expression.
source: Although the mechanistic basis for how cell shape regulates RELA remains poorly understood, studies have shown that chemically inhibiting actin or tubulin dynamics can increase RELA binding to DNA and RELA-dependent gene expression (Rosette and Karin, 1995; Bourgarel-Rey et al., 2001; Németh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rosette and Karin, 1995; Bourgarel-Rey et al., 2001; Németh et al., 2004.

claim: TNFα and RELA are frequently upregulated in PDAC tumours.
source: Despite frequent upregulation of both TNFα and RELA in PDAC tumours (Weichert et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2016), the dynamics and regulation of single-cell RELA translocation, as well as RELA transcriptional output, are poorly understood for PDAC cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weichert et al., 2007 and Zhao et al., 2016.

claim: MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells harbour key genomic alterations in PDAC, including KRAS and p53 mutations and homozygous deletions in CDKN2A/p16.
source: To study PDAC biology, we used the frequently studied human PDAC cell lines MIA PaCa2 and PANC1, which harbour key genomic alterations in PDAC, including KRAS and p53 mutations and homozygous deletions in CDKN2A/p16 (Deer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Deer et al., 2010.

claim: MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells are epithelial in origin but have distinct cell morphologies.
source: In addition, MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells are epithelial in origin but have distinct cell morphologies and are therefore useful for analysis of cell shape interaction with RELA.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the cell lines used in the study.

claim: RELA was tagged at the C-terminus to avoid interference with the N-terminal Rel homology domain.
source: The C-terminus was selected to avoid interference with the N-terminal Rel homology domain, which contains the transactivation, nuclear import and DNA-binding domains (Kieran et al., 1990; Nolan et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citations to Kieran et al., 1990 and Nolan et al., 1991.

claim: The N-terminal Rel homology domain contains the transactivation, nuclear import and DNA-binding domains.
source: The C-terminus was selected to avoid interference with the N-terminal Rel homology domain, which contains the transactivation, nuclear import and DNA-binding domains (Kieran et al., 1990; Nolan et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kieran et al., 1990 and Nolan et al., 1991.

claim: PCNA is a processivity factor for DNA polymerase δ that functions during replication.
source: We also introduced mScarlet-I to the C-terminus of PCNA (proliferating cell nuclear antigen; abbreviated as PCNA-Scarlet) – a processivity factor for DNA polymerase δ that functions during replication – which served as a nuclear marker for segmentation and as a cell cycle marker (Kurki et al., 1986; Barr et al., 2017; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kurki et al., 1986 and Barr et al., 2017.

claim: MIA PaCa2 cells responded with higher nuclear RELA compared to PANC1 cells at each TNFα dose.
source: MIA PaCa2 cells responded with higher nuclear RELA compared to PANC1 cells at each TNFα dose (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 1C from live imaging experiments.

claim: Peak nuclear RELA was statistically significantly different between 0.01 and 0.1 ng/ml for MIA PaCa2 but not for PANC1 cells.
source: Peak nuclear RELA, quantified as the first timepoint at which the slope of the single-cell RELA track ≤ 0, was statistically significantly different between 0.01 and 0.1 ng/ml for MIA PaCa2 but not for PANC1 cells, suggesting that MIA PaCa2 cells are more sensitive to TNFα dose in terms of RELA activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: MIA PaCa2 cells are more sensitive to TNFα dose in terms of RELA activation.
source: Peak nuclear RELA, quantified as the first timepoint at which the slope of the single-cell RELA track ≤ 0, was statistically significantly different between 0.01 and 0.1 ng/ml for MIA PaCa2 but not for PANC1 cells, suggesting that MIA PaCa2 cells are more sensitive to TNFα dose in terms of RELA activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical analysis results.

claim: 10 ng/ml TNFα elicited a significantly higher nuclear RELA localisation amplitude in both cell lines compared to lower TNFα doses.
source: 10 ng/ml TNFα elicited a significantly higher nuclear RELA localisation amplitude in both cell lines compared to lower TNFα doses (0.01 and 0.1 ng/ml).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: TNFα dose did not affect the time to peak RELA in MIA PaCa2 cells.
source: In contrast, TNFα dose did not affect the time to peak RELA in MIA PaCa2 cells, while PANC1 cells displayed a slower time to peak at 0.01 ng/ml TNFα compared to higher doses (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PANC1 cells displayed a slower time to peak at 0.01 ng/ml TNFα compared to higher doses.
source: In contrast, TNFα dose did not affect the time to peak RELA in MIA PaCa2 cells, while PANC1 cells displayed a slower time to peak at 0.01 ng/ml TNFα compared to higher doses (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In MIA PaCa2 cells, there is a high correlation between nuclear RELA at later timepoints (180, 300, or 600 min) compared to an early timepoint (60 min) following TNFα addition.
source: In MIA PaCa2 cells, there is a high correlation between nuclear RELA at later timepoints (180, 300, or 600 min) compared to an early timepoint (60 min) following TNFα addition.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of single-cell tracking data.

claim: PANC1 cells have high correlation between nuclear RELA measurements at 60 min RELA and 180 min, while there is weak correlation between RELA levels at 60 and 600 min.
source: PANC1 cells have high correlation between nuclear RELA measurements at 60 min RELA and 180 min, while there is weak correlation between RELA levels at 60 and 600 min.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of single-cell tracking data.

claim: In MIA PaCa2, RELA translocation at 60 min is largely predictive of the long-term response to TNFα.
source: Thus, in MIA PaCa2, but not PANC1, RELA translocation at 60 min is largely predictive of the long-term response to TNFα and MIA PaCa2 cells maintain TNFα-induced nuclear RELA levels for an extended duration (10 hr) following exposure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis results.

claim: MIA PaCa2 cells maintain TNFα-induced nuclear RELA levels for an extended duration (10 hr) following exposure.
source: Thus, in MIA PaCa2, but not PANC1, RELA translocation at 60 min is largely predictive of the long-term response to TNFα and MIA PaCa2 cells maintain TNFα-induced nuclear RELA levels for an extended duration (10 hr) following exposure.
evidence: This is based on analysis of time-course imaging data.

claim: RELA nuclear translocation occurs rapidly in both MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells in response to TNFα.
source: Overall, our data show that RELA nuclear translocation occurs rapidly, and with non-oscillatory dynamics in both MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells in response to TNFα.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: RELA nuclear translocation is largely sustained for hours in MIA PaCa2 cells, while damped in PANC1 cells.
source: Nuclear RELA translocation is largely sustained for hours in MIA PaCa2 cells, while damped in PANC1 cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: There were minimal differences between cells by cell cycle stage in terms of peak RELA measurements in MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells.
source: Largely, there were minimal differences between cells by cell cycle stage in terms of peak RELA measurements (amplitude or timing) in MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), with the exception of statistically significant lower peak RELA amplitude detected in G2 cells compared to S phase cells only, and exclusively for the MIA PaCa2 cell line at 10 ng/ml TNFα.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Nuclear RELA translocation in response to TNFα in PDAC cells appears to be largely cell cycle independent.
source: Overall, nuclear RELA translocation in response to TNFα in PDAC cells appears to be largely cell cycle independent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell cycle analysis data.

claim: Nuclear RELA was statistically predicted as dependent on actin features across Bayesian models.
source: Notably, nuclear RELA was statistically predicted as dependent on actin features across Bayesian models.
evidence: This is based on Bayesian network modeling results.

claim: Nuclear RELA measurements are correlated to and predicted to be dependent on cytoplasmic actin and tubulin intensity.
source: This model indicated that nuclear RELA measurements are correlated to and predicted to be dependent on cytoplasmic actin and tubulin intensity, suggesting that cytoskeletal dynamics influence heterogeneity in nuclear RELA translocation with TNFα.
evidence: This is based on the Bayesian network model shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cytoskeletal dynamics influence heterogeneity in nuclear RELA translocation with TNFα.
source: This model indicated that nuclear RELA measurements are correlated to and predicted to be dependent on cytoplasmic actin and tubulin intensity, suggesting that cytoskeletal dynamics influence heterogeneity in nuclear RELA translocation with TNFα.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayesian modeling results.

claim: Nuclear RELA is predicted to be dependent on cell area.
source: Nuclear RELA is also predicted to be dependent on cell area, although with a lower strength of the probabilistic relationship compared to actin/tubulin, while nucleus roundness is predicted to be dependent on nuclear RELA.
evidence: This is based on the Bayesian network model.

claim: Nucleus roundness is predicted to be dependent on nuclear RELA.
source: Nuclear RELA is also predicted to be dependent on cell area, although with a lower strength of the probabilistic relationship compared to actin/tubulin, while nucleus roundness is predicted to be dependent on nuclear RELA.
evidence: This is based on the Bayesian network model.

claim: Both actin texture and the ratio of membrane to cytoplasm actin are predicted to be dependent on RELA.
source: Interestingly, both actin texture and the ratio of membrane to cytoplasm actin are also predicted to be dependent on RELA, suggesting that RELA and actin dynamics are interdependent.
evidence: This is based on the Bayesian network model.

claim: RELA and actin dynamics are interdependent.
source: Interestingly, both actin texture and the ratio of membrane to cytoplasm actin are also predicted to be dependent on RELA, suggesting that RELA and actin dynamics are interdependent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayesian modeling results.

claim: The influence of cell shape on RELA translocation is likely mediated through cytoskeletal changes.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that the influence of cell shape on RELA translocation we have previously described in breast cancer cells (Sero et al., 2015; Sailem and Bakal, 2017) is likely mediated through cytoskeletal changes.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining current findings with previous work.

claim: There is a general lack of dependence of nuclear RELA on cell shape features in PDAC cells.
source: In contrast to our prior findings using Bayesian modelling of RELA and cell shape with breast cancer cells in the absence of cytoskeletal measurements (Sero et al., 2015; Sailem and Bakal, 2017), here we found a general lack of dependence of nuclear RELA on cell shape features, but identified strong and consistent dependencies of nuclear RELA on cytoplasm actin and tubulin, as well as actin texture, in several PDAC cell lines and TNFα doses (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Strong and consistent dependencies of nuclear RELA on cytoplasm actin and tubulin were identified in several PDAC cell lines and TNFα doses.
source: In contrast to our prior findings using Bayesian modelling of RELA and cell shape with breast cancer cells in the absence of cytoskeletal measurements (Sero et al., 2015; Sailem and Bakal, 2017), here we found a general lack of dependence of nuclear RELA on cell shape features, but identified strong and consistent dependencies of nuclear RELA on cytoplasm actin and tubulin, as well as actin texture, in several PDAC cell lines and TNFα doses (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Actin and tubulin abundance and actin distribution within the cell influence RELA nuclear translocation.
source: These data computationally predict that actin and tubulin abundance and actin distribution within the cell influence RELA nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayesian modeling results.

claim: Following drug-treatment, only 'cytoplasmic actin mean' remained as an influencing variable on RELA.
source: Interestingly, the Bayesian network following perturbations revealed that 5/6 of the variables observed to correlate with RELA (whether they influenced RELA or were influenced by RELA) in untreated cells were independent of RELA in the drug-treated network. Only 'cytoplasmic actin mean' remained as an influencing variable following drug-treatment, suggesting that actin abundance is a key regulator of RELA nuclear localisation.
evidence: This is based on Bayesian modeling with drug perturbation data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Actin abundance is a key regulator of RELA nuclear localisation.
source: Interestingly, the Bayesian network following perturbations revealed that 5/6 of the variables observed to correlate with RELA (whether they influenced RELA or were influenced by RELA) in untreated cells were independent of RELA in the drug-treated network. Only 'cytoplasmic actin mean' remained as an influencing variable following drug-treatment, suggesting that actin abundance is a key regulator of RELA nuclear localisation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayesian modeling results with drug perturbations.

claim: Other variables (i.e. tubulin and cell shape) can indirectly influence RELA via regulating actin network organisation.
source: While other variables (i.e. tubulin and cell shape) can indirectly influence RELA, they do so via regulating actin network organisation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayesian modeling results.

claim: A total of 254 genes were differentially expressed in high TNFα (0.1 or 10 ng/ml) versus basal conditions.
source: A total of 254 genes were differentially expressed in high TNFα (0.1 or 10 ng/ml) versus basal conditions, with the majority of genes (186) upregulated by TNFα (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The majority of genes (186) were upregulated by TNFα.
source: A total of 254 genes were differentially expressed in high TNFα (0.1 or 10 ng/ml) versus basal conditions, with the majority of genes (186) upregulated by TNFα (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Cluster 3 shows genes with clear dependence on RELA activation in both MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells.
source: Cluster 3 shows genes with clear dependence on RELA activation in both MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells and has genes significantly upregulated by TNFα in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq clustering analysis shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Cluster 3 genes are more highly upregulated by TNFα in MIA PaCa2 compared to PANC1 cells.
source: Moreover, cluster 3 genes are more highly upregulated by TNFα in MIA PaCa2 compared to PANC1 cells, which is consistent with the RELA dynamics observed by live imaging whereby 0.1 ng/ml is sufficient to increase RELA nuclear localisation in MIA PaCa2 but not PANC1 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data and is consistent with live imaging data in Figure 1D.

claim: Cluster 3 genes have higher RELA expression at 5 hr TNFα compared to 1 hr TNFα in both cell lines.
source: Cluster 3 genes also have higher RELA expression at 5 hr TNFα compared to 1 hr TNFα in both cell lines, indicating that they are associated with prolonged RELA activation.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq time-course data.

claim: Known RELA targets such as RELB, NFKB2, and BIRC3 are present in cluster 3.
source: As expected from the RELA and TNFα dose-dependent properties of this cluster, known RELA targets such as RELB, NFKB2, and BIRC3 are present (Lombardi et al., 1995; Bren et al., 2001; Frasor et al., 2009), and also have the immune ligands CD70 and CD83.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data and supported by citations to Lombardi et al., 1995; Bren et al., 2001; Frasor et al., 2009.

claim: Cluster 3 contains ARHGAP31 and NUAK2, which are involved in the regulation of actin.
source: Notably, cluster 3 contains Rho GTPase-activating protein 31 (ARHGAP31) and NUAK family kinase 2 (NUAK2), which are involved in the regulation of actin (Tcherkezian et al., 2006; Vallenius et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data and supported by citations to Tcherkezian et al., 2006 and Vallenius et al., 2011.

claim: Cluster 1 consists of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs).
source: Cluster 1 consists of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and is further downregulated by IκB-SR in the MIA PaCa2 cell line only, suggesting that RELA and TNFα have antagonistic effects on the expression of these lncRNAs.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq clustering analysis.

claim: RELA and TNFα have antagonistic effects on the expression of cluster 1 lncRNAs.
source: Cluster 1 consists of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and is further downregulated by IκB-SR in the MIA PaCa2 cell line only, suggesting that RELA and TNFα have antagonistic effects on the expression of these lncRNAs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNA-seq data with IκB-SR.

claim: Cluster 2 genes are entirely independent of RELA.
source: In contrast, cluster 2 genes are entirely independent of RELA.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq clustering analysis.

claim: TNFα/RELA dynamics determine transcriptional output in PDAC cells.
source: Overall, we identified gene expression patterns linked to TNFα dose and duration, as well as variable dependence on RELA, suggesting that TNFα/RELA dynamics determine transcriptional output in PDAC cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Expression of RELA itself did not significantly scale with TNFα dose.
source: RNA-seq in MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells revealed that expression of RELA itself did not significantly scale with TNFα dose, while RELB and the transcriptionally incompetent NF-κB proteins NFKB1 and NFKB2 showed increasing expression with increasing TNFα (left graph in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RELB and the transcriptionally incompetent NF-κB proteins NFKB1 and NFKB2 showed increasing expression with increasing TNFα.
source: RNA-seq in MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells revealed that expression of RELA itself did not significantly scale with TNFα dose, while RELB and the transcriptionally incompetent NF-κB proteins NFKB1 and NFKB2 showed increasing expression with increasing TNFα (left graph in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RELB, REL, NFKB2, and NFKBIE have reduced expression with IκB-SR induction in both MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells.
source: We compared RNA expression in TNFα-treated cells between cells with or without IκB-SR induction (Wilcoxon tests with multiple test correction), which revealed that RELB, REL, NFKB2, and NFKBIE have reduced expression with IκB-SR induction in both MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A').
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A'.

claim: The expression of RELB, REL, NFKB2, and NFKBIE relies on nuclear translocation of RELA.
source: These findings indicate that the expression of these genes relies on nuclear translocation of RELA, while the other NF-κB and IκB genes, including the canonical RELA binding partner NFKB1, do not require RELA activation for expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the IκB-SR RNA-seq data.

claim: The expression of NF-κB or IκB genes did not show any statistically significant differences between the 1 and 5 hr TNFα treatments.
source: In both MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells, the expression of NF-κB or IκB genes did not show any statistically significant differences between the 1 and 5 hr TNFα treatments.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of RNA-seq time-course data.

claim: NF-κB and IκB genes are 'early' genes upregulated rapidly and consistently following TNFα treatment.
source: These results are in line with previous findings that NF-κB and IκB genes are 'early' genes upregulated rapidly and consistently following TNFα treatment (Tian et al., 2005; Tay et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tian et al., 2005 and Tay et al., 2010.

claim: GFP-Trap followed by mass spectrometry with MIA PaCa2 cells expressing endogenously tagged RELA-GFP pulled down six NF-κB/IκB proteins.
source: GFP-Trap followed by mass spectrometry with MIA PaCa2 cells expressing endogenously tagged RELA-GFP pulled down six NF-κB/IκB proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on Co-IP and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IκBα/NFKBIA, IκBβ/NFKBIB, and IκBε/NFKBIE were pulled down at lower abundance with increasing TNFα dose.
source: IκBα/NFKBIA, IκBβ/NFKBIB, and IκBε/NFKBIE were pulled down at lower abundance with increasing TNFα dose, in line with the well-studied degradation of IκB proteins downstream of TNFα stimulation (Chen et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on Co-IP/mass spectrometry data and supported by a citation to Chen et al., 1995.

claim: The NF-κB protein REL had reduced interaction with RELA with TNFα.
source: Interestingly, the NF-κB protein REL also had reduced interaction with RELA with TNFα.
evidence: This is based on Co-IP/mass spectrometry data.

claim: NFKB1 and NFKB2 showed increased interaction with RELA with TNFα.
source: In contrast, NFKB1 and NFKB2 showed increased interaction with RELA with TNFα.
evidence: This is based on Co-IP/mass spectrometry data.

claim: RELA forms NF-κB heterodimers with REL, NFKB1 and NFKB2 in PDAC cells.
source: RELA therefore appears to form NF-κB heterodimers with REL, NFKB1 and NFKB2 in PDAC cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Co-IP/mass spectrometry data.

claim: RELA siRNA abrogated the nuclear RELA signal.
source: We used non-targeting (NT) siRNA as a negative control for comparison and verified transfection efficacy using RELA siRNA, which abrogated the nuclear RELA signal ('RELA' panels in Figure 4A), in addition to qRT-PCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which showed on-target reduction in RNA expression by each siRNA.
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RELA siRNA demonstrated the most significant reduction in the AUC of nuclear RELA signal compared to the non-targeting siRNA in both cell lines in both basal conditions and with TNFα.
source: As expected, RELA siRNA demonstrated the most significant reduction in the AUC of nuclear RELA signal compared to the non-targeting siRNA in both cell lines in both basal conditions and with TNFα.
evidence: This is based on AUC analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Depletion of NFKBIB caused significant upregulation RELA responsiveness (fold-change) to TNFα in both cell lines.
source: In both cell lines, depletion of NFKBIB also caused significant upregulation RELA responsiveness (fold-change) to TNFα, while PANC1 cells also displayed RELA upregulation with NFKBIA or ARHGAP31 depletion and RELA downregulation with NFKB2 depletion.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of AUC data from siRNA experiments.

claim: IκBβ plays a significant role in suppressing TNFα induction of nuclear RELA in PDAC cells.
source: These results suggest that IκBβ plays a significant role in suppressing TNFα induction of nuclear RELA in PDAC cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the siRNA knockdown results.

claim: Nuclear RELA AUC in control conditions was affected by all of the tested NF-κB pathway components in PANC1 cells.
source: Interestingly, nuclear RELA AUC in control conditions was affected by all of the tested NF-κB pathway components in PANC1 cells, indicating that RELA is highly modulated by NF-κB/IκB proteins in the absence of stress or inflammatory cues.
evidence: This is based on AUC analysis of siRNA knockdown data.

claim: RELA is highly modulated by NF-κB/IκB proteins in the absence of stress or inflammatory cues in PANC1 cells.
source: Interestingly, nuclear RELA AUC in control conditions was affected by all of the tested NF-κB pathway components in PANC1 cells, indicating that RELA is highly modulated by NF-κB/IκB proteins in the absence of stress or inflammatory cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the siRNA knockdown results.

claim: ARHGAP31 regulates both the 1 hr and 12 hr levels of nuclear RELA fold-change (TNFα/control) in both MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells.
source: Of note, Wilcoxon tests with multiple test correction showed that ARHGAP31 regulates both the 1 hr and 12 hr levels of nuclear RELA fold-change (TNFα/control) in both MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of siRNA knockdown data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: ARHGAP31 depletion upregulated nuclear RELA localisation in response to TNFα.
source: In general, ARHGAP31 depletion upregulated nuclear RELA localisation in response to TNFα, suggesting that ARHGAP31 suppresses inflammatory activation of RELA.
evidence: This is based on siRNA knockdown experimental data.

claim: ARHGAP31 suppresses inflammatory activation of RELA.
source: In general, ARHGAP31 depletion upregulated nuclear RELA localisation in response to TNFα, suggesting that ARHGAP31 suppresses inflammatory activation of RELA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the siRNA knockdown results.

claim: NUAK2 depletion upregulates nuclear RELA following 1 hr TNFα in PANC1 cells.
source: NUAK2 depletion upregulates nuclear RELA following 1 hr TNFα in PANC1 cells, but downregulates nuclear RELA following 12 hr TNFα in MIA PaCa2 cells.
evidence: This is based on siRNA knockdown experimental data.

claim: NUAK2 depletion downregulates nuclear RELA following 12 hr TNFα in MIA PaCa2 cells.
source: NUAK2 depletion upregulates nuclear RELA following 1 hr TNFα in PANC1 cells, but downregulates nuclear RELA following 12 hr TNFα in MIA PaCa2 cells.
evidence: This is based on siRNA knockdown experimental data.

claim: The dynamics between RELA with NUAK2 are both cell line and time-dependent.
source: These results suggest that the dynamics between RELA with NUAK2 are complex as they are both cell line and time-dependent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the siRNA knockdown results.

claim: RELB depletion significantly affected the RELA response to TNFα in the MIA PaCa2 cell line.
source: In terms of knockdown of NF-κB protein encoding genes, depletion of the non-canonical gene RELB significantly affected the RELA response to TNFα in the MIA PaCa2 cell line, with RELB depletion downregulating nuclear RELA (fold-change) at 1 hr and upregulating nuclear RELA (fold-change) at 12 hr, suggesting that RELB regulates both the 'early' and 'late' nuclear translocation responses of RELA to TNFα in MIA PaCa2 cells.
evidence: This is based on siRNA knockdown experimental data.

claim: RELB regulates both the 'early' and 'late' nuclear translocation responses of RELA to TNFα in MIA PaCa2 cells.
source: In terms of knockdown of NF-κB protein encoding genes, depletion of the non-canonical gene RELB significantly affected the RELA response to TNFα in the MIA PaCa2 cell line, with RELB depletion downregulating nuclear RELA (fold-change) at 1 hr and upregulating nuclear RELA (fold-change) at 12 hr, suggesting that RELB regulates both the 'early' and 'late' nuclear translocation responses of RELA to TNFα in MIA PaCa2 cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the siRNA knockdown results.

claim: The knockdown of several NF-κB/IκB genes upregulated nuclear RELA in PANC1 cells with 12 hr treatment: NFKBIA, NFKBIB, NFKBIE, and RELB.
source: While no NF-κB pathway components appear to regulate the fold-change of nuclear RELA in PANC1 cells to 1 hr TNFα, the knockdown of several NF-κB/IκB genes upregulated nuclear RELA in PANC1 cells with 12 hr treatment: NFKBIA, NFKBIB, NFKBIE, and RELB.
evidence: This is based on siRNA knockdown experimental data.

claim: IκBβ plays a role specifically in the 'late' response of RELA to TNFα in PANC1 cells.
source: Finally, the fold-change in nuclear RELA signal with 12 hr TNFα was significantly upregulated by NFKBIB depletion in PANC1 cells, suggesting that IκBβ plays a role specifically in the 'late' response of RELA to TNFα in this cell line.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the siRNA knockdown results.

claim: PDAC cells show atypical RELA dynamics compared to reports in cells from other tissues.
source: Strikingly, PDAC cells show atypical RELA dynamics compared to reports in cells from other tissues (Ashall et al., 2009; Tay et al., 2010; Sero et al., 2015), as we observed that PDAC cells maintain prolonged nuclear RELA localisation and RELA responses are cell cycle independent.
evidence: This is a comparison of current findings with previous literature.

claim: MIA PaCa2 cells respond with higher and sustained RELA nuclear localisation compared to PANC1 cells.
source: However, we identified that a key difference between MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells is that MIA PaCa2 cells respond with higher and sustained RELA nuclear localisation compared to PANC1 cells, while PANC1 cells have a damped RELA response over time.
evidence: This is based on live imaging experimental data.

claim: RELA nuclear translocation in PDAC cells occurs immediately following TNFα addition.
source: Similar to other cell lines (Ashall et al., 2009; Tay et al., 2010; Sero et al., 2015), we found that RELA nuclear translocation in PDAC cells occurs immediately following TNFα addition and peak nuclear RELA localisation occurs around 1 hr post-TNFα.
evidence: This is based on live imaging data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Peak nuclear RELA localisation occurs around 1 hr post-TNFα in PDAC cells.
source: Similar to other cell lines (Ashall et al., 2009; Tay et al., 2010; Sero et al., 2015), we found that RELA nuclear translocation in PDAC cells occurs immediately following TNFα addition and peak nuclear RELA localisation occurs around 1 hr post-TNFα.
evidence: This is based on live imaging data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The distinct RELA dynamics between PDAC cells with reports from other tissues may be attributed to the use of knock-in RELA-GFP in this study.
source: The distinct RELA dynamics between PDAC cells with reports from other tissues may be attributed to the use of knock-in RELA-GFP in this study since many studies used exogenous RELA fusion constructs (Ashall et al., 2009; Tay et al., 2010; Sero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about methodological differences.

claim: Other studies that have tagged RELA endogenously did detect oscillations, including MEFs and MCF7 breast cancer cells.
source: Nonetheless, other studies that have tagged RELA endogenously did detect oscillations, including MEFs (Sung et al., 2009; Zambrano et al., 2016) and MCF7 breast cancer cells (Stewart-Ornstein and Lahav, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sung et al., 2009; Zambrano et al., 2016; Stewart-Ornstein and Lahav, 2016.

claim: MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells in all cell cycle stages are responsive to 0.1 and 10 ng/ml TNFα.
source: Here, we identified that MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells in all cell cycle stages are responsive to 0.1 and 10 ng/ml TNFα, with minimal dissimilarities in RELA translocation responses between cell cycle stages in terms of mean nuclear RELA or the amplitude and timing of peak RELA.
evidence: This is based on cell cycle analysis of live imaging data.

claim: RELA translocation responses to TNFα were identified in HeLa cells as dependent on the cell cycle phase at the time of TNFα addition.
source: In contrast, RELA translocation responses to TNFα were identified in HeLa cells by Ankers et al., 2016 as dependent on the cell cycle phase at the time of TNFα addition in a study using double thymidine block to synchronise cells, or Fluorescent Ubiquitination-based Cell Cycle Indicator (FUCCI) labelling to infer cell cycle phase.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ankers et al., 2016.

claim: HeLa cells treated with 10 ng/ml TNFα in late G1 displayed a stronger response than the population average.
source: HeLa cells treated with 10 ng/ml TNFα in late G1 displayed a stronger response than the population average, while S-phase cells showed a suppressed or delayed response.
evidence: This is based on findings from Ankers et al., 2016.

claim: RELA was found to interact with E2F1 in late G1 when E2F1 levels are highest during the cell cycle.
source: Furthermore, RELA was found to interact with E2F1, a transcription factor regulating the G1 to S transition, in late G1 when E2F1 levels are highest during the cell cycle (Ankers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ankers et al., 2016.

claim: Conflicting reports of whether TNFα-induced RELA translocation is cell cycle regulated may be due to cancer cell type-specific deregulation of cell cycle proteins.
source: Conflicting reports of whether TNFα-induced RELA translocation is cell cycle regulated may be due to cancer cell type-specific deregulation of cell cycle proteins (Cordon-Cardo, 1995; Otto and Sicinski, 2017) or RELA may not physically interact with E2F1 in PDAC cells in general or specifically in unsynchronised cells.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations.

claim: The high sensitivity of PDAC cells to TNFα and lack of oscillations suggest that PDAC cells may suppress negative feedback imposed by IκBα.
source: The high sensitivity of PDAC cells to TNFα and lack of oscillations suggest that PDAC cells may suppress negative feedback imposed by IκBα, as Hoffmann et al., 2002 demonstrated that oscillations in NF-κB DNA binding are due to negative feedback with IκBα, which is encoded by a gene (NFKBIA) upregulated by NF-κB factors.
evidence: This is speculation based on current findings and previous literature.

claim: Oscillations in NF-κB DNA binding are due to negative feedback with IκBα.
source: The high sensitivity of PDAC cells to TNFα and lack of oscillations suggest that PDAC cells may suppress negative feedback imposed by IκBα, as Hoffmann et al., 2002 demonstrated that oscillations in NF-κB DNA binding are due to negative feedback with IκBα, which is encoded by a gene (NFKBIA) upregulated by NF-κB factors.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoffmann et al., 2002.

claim: Cells with high IκBβ and IκBε expression, or absence of IκBα, lose oscillations stimulated by TNFα.
source: Hoffman et al. also identified that cells with high IκBβ and IκBε expression, or absence of IκBα, lose oscillations stimulated by TNFα.
evidence: This is based on findings from Hoffmann et al., 2002.

claim: RELA binds to IκBα, IκBβ, and IκBε in MIA PaCa2 cells.
source: Using co-immunoprecipitation of RELA with MIA PaCa2 cells, we found that RELA binds to IκBα, IκBβ, and IκBε and binding to each is suppressed in high TNFα concentrations.
evidence: This is based on Co-IP experimental data.

claim: Binding of RELA to IκBα, IκBβ, and IκBε is suppressed in high TNFα concentrations.
source: Using co-immunoprecipitation of RELA with MIA PaCa2 cells, we found that RELA binds to IκBα, IκBβ, and IκBε and binding to each is suppressed in high TNFα concentrations.
evidence: This is based on Co-IP experimental data.

claim: The lack of RELA oscillations in MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells may be due to enhanced positive feedback and/or insufficient NFKBIA expression.
source: However, contrary to our expectations based on the findings by Hoffmann et al., we did not observe RELA oscillations with NFKBIB or NFKBIE depletion in MIA PaCa2 or PANC1 cells, suggesting that the lack of RELA oscillations in these cell lines may be due to enhanced positive feedback and/or insufficient NFKBIA expression.
evidence: This is speculation based on siRNA knockdown results.

claim: The relative abundance of the RelA:c-Rel dimer was higher in the nucleus of resting cells then higher in the cytoplasm of TNFα-stimulated cells.
source: This is in line with a recent study (Rahman et al., 2022) that endogenously fluorescently labelled RelA and c-Rel in double knockin mice and used fluorescence cross-correlation spectroscopy to probe for binding/dimerisation in primary ear fibroblasts to quantify the abundance of RelA:c-Rel heterodimers pre- and post-TNFα. Rahman et al., 2022 identified that the relative abundance of the RelA:c-Rel dimer was higher in the nucleus of resting cells then higher in the cytoplasm of TNFα-stimulated cells, despite the individual concentrations of RelA and c-Rel increasing in the nucleus with TNFα.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rahman et al., 2022.

claim: Binding of RELA and REL is reduced with TNFα in multiple cell types and in both human and mouse models.
source: Our combined results suggest that binding of RELA and REL is reduced with TNFα in multiple cell types and in both human and mouse models.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining current Co-IP data with previous literature.

claim: Differences in cytoplasmic actin intensity were predictive of differences in nuclear RELA between single PDAC cells.
source: Consistently among our models, differences in cytoplasmic actin intensity, as well as measures of actin localisation (cortical versus cytoplasmic actin), were predictive of differences in nuclear RELA between single PDAC cells.
evidence: This is based on Bayesian modeling results.

claim: Measures of actin localisation (cortical versus cytoplasmic actin) were predictive of differences in nuclear RELA between single PDAC cells.
source: Consistently among our models, differences in cytoplasmic actin intensity, as well as measures of actin localisation (cortical versus cytoplasmic actin), were predictive of differences in nuclear RELA between single PDAC cells.
evidence: This is based on Bayesian modeling results.

claim: Cytoskeletal structures may influence RELA dynamics by inducing changes in TNF receptor turnover or conformation.
source: One route through which cytoskeletal structures may influence RELA dynamics is by inducing changes in TNF receptor turnover or conformation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: The actin-binding protein Filamin interacts with TNF receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2).
source: One example is that the actin-binding protein Filamin interacts with TNF receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2), which is not itself a TNF receptor but is involved in TNF receptor intracellular signal transduction (Leonardi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leonardi et al., 2000.

claim: Space confinement of dendritic cells leads to upregulation of the chemokine receptor Ccr7 in a manner dependent on expression and function of IKKβ and the lipid metabolism enzyme cPLA2.
source: On a related topic, a recently published study (Alraies et al., 2024) subjected dendritic cells to space confinement and found upregulation of the chemokine receptor Ccr7, in a manner dependent on expression and function of IKKβ and the lipid metabolism enzyme cPLA2.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alraies et al., 2024.

claim: The prostaglandin E2 receptor (PGE2) receptor induces NF-κB nuclear translocation.
source: In turn, the prostaglandin E2 receptor (PGE2) receptor, which is in the cPLA2 pathway, induces NF-κB nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is based on findings from Alraies et al., 2024.

claim: ARP2/3 activity regulates cPLA2 activation via nuclear envelope tensioning.
source: This study also identifies the role of ARP2/3 activity in regulating cPLA2 activation via nuclear envelope tensioning.
evidence: This is based on findings from Alraies et al., 2024.

claim: 254 genes significantly regulated by TNFα may be viewed as candidates for targeting NF-κB signalling or output in PDAC.
source: To identify potential regulatory loops involving RELA in PDAC, we used RNA-seq analysis with MIA PaCa2 and PANC1 cells treated with varying TNFα doses +/-IκB-SR. We identified 254 genes significantly regulated by TNFα, which may be viewed as candidates for targeting NF-κB signalling or output in PDAC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNA-seq results.

claim: The 5-year survival rate of non-resected PDAC patients has remained unchanged from 1975 to 2011.
source: Identifying novel targets for PDAC is important as the 5-year survival rate of non-resected PDAC patients has remained unchanged from 1975 to 2011 (Bengtsson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bengtsson et al., 2020.

claim: RELA is hyperactive in 50–70% of PDAC tumours.
source: Moreover, RELA is hyperactive in 50–70% of PDAC tumours (Wang et al., 1999; Weichert et al., 2007) and contributes to both cancer progression (Fujioka et al., 2003; Melisi et al., 2009) and resistance to chemotherapy (Bold et al., 2001; Kunnumakkara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 1999 and Weichert et al., 2007.

claim: RELA contributes to cancer progression in PDAC.
source: Moreover, RELA is hyperactive in 50–70% of PDAC tumours (Wang et al., 1999; Weichert et al., 2007) and contributes to both cancer progression (Fujioka et al., 2003; Melisi et al., 2009) and resistance to chemotherapy (Bold et al., 2001; Kunnumakkara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fujioka et al., 2003 and Melisi et al., 2009.

claim: RELA contributes to resistance to chemotherapy in PDAC.
source: Moreover, RELA is hyperactive in 50–70% of PDAC tumours (Wang et al., 1999; Weichert et al., 2007) and contributes to both cancer progression (Fujioka et al., 2003; Melisi et al., 2009) and resistance to chemotherapy (Bold et al., 2001; Kunnumakkara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bold et al., 2001 and Kunnumakkara et al., 2007.

claim: This is the first evidence that ARHGAP31 is a transcriptional target of TNFα or RELA.
source: Of note, we present the first evidence that ARHGAP31 is a transcriptional target of TNFα or RELA.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on RNA-seq data.

claim: ARHGAP31 is not previously associated with pancreatic cancer.
source: Moreover, ARHGAP31 is not previously associated with pancreatic cancer, but has well-studied roles in actin modulation, since ARHGAP31 is the human orthologue for the mouse protein CdGAP (mCdc42 GTPase-activating protein) and ARHGAP31 inactivates the GTPases CDC42 and RAC1 (Lamarche-Vane and Hall, 1998; Tcherkezian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature and is supported by citations.

claim: ARHGAP31 is the human orthologue for the mouse protein CdGAP (mCdc42 GTPase-activating protein).
source: Moreover, ARHGAP31 is not previously associated with pancreatic cancer, but has well-studied roles in actin modulation, since ARHGAP31 is the human orthologue for the mouse protein CdGAP (mCdc42 GTPase-activating protein) and ARHGAP31 inactivates the GTPases CDC42 and RAC1 (Lamarche-Vane and Hall, 1998; Tcherkezian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lamarche-Vane and Hall, 1998 and Tcherkezian et al., 2006.

claim: ARHGAP31 inactivates the GTPases CDC42 and RAC1.
source: Moreover, ARHGAP31 is not previously associated with pancreatic cancer, but has well-studied roles in actin modulation, since ARHGAP31 is the human orthologue for the mouse protein CdGAP (mCdc42 GTPase-activating protein) and ARHGAP31 inactivates the GTPases CDC42 and RAC1 (Lamarche-Vane and Hall, 1998; Tcherkezian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lamarche-Vane and Hall, 1998 and Tcherkezian et al., 2006.

claim: CDC42 is involved in the formation of premigratory filopodia in PDAC cells and promotes invasiveness.
source: CDC42 is involved in the formation of premigratory filopodia in PDAC cells and promotes invasiveness (Razidlo et al., 2018), while RAC1 expression is required for the development of PDAC tumours, in addition to the formation of the ADM and PanIN precursors in KRASG12D mouse models (Heid et al., 2011), indicating that RAC1 may play a role in actin remodelling during PDAC initiation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Razidlo et al., 2018.

claim: RAC1 expression is required for the development of PDAC tumours.
source: CDC42 is involved in the formation of premigratory filopodia in PDAC cells and promotes invasiveness (Razidlo et al., 2018), while RAC1 expression is required for the development of PDAC tumours, in addition to the formation of the ADM and PanIN precursors in KRASG12D mouse models (Heid et al., 2011), indicating that RAC1 may play a role in actin remodelling during PDAC initiation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heid et al., 2011.

claim: RAC1 may play a role in actin remodelling during PDAC initiation.
source: CDC42 is involved in the formation of premigratory filopodia in PDAC cells and promotes invasiveness (Razidlo et al., 2018), while RAC1 expression is required for the development of PDAC tumours, in addition to the formation of the ADM and PanIN precursors in KRASG12D mouse models (Heid et al., 2011), indicating that RAC1 may play a role in actin remodelling during PDAC initiation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on findings from Heid et al., 2011.

claim: TNFα upregulates RNA expression of the kinase-encoding gene NUAK2 (SNARK).
source: Our results also demonstrate that TNFα upregulates RNA expression of the kinase-encoding gene NUAK2 (SNARK), while NUAK2 expression is abrogated in the presence of IκB-SR.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claim: NUAK2 expression is abrogated in the presence of IκB-SR.
source: Our results also demonstrate that TNFα upregulates RNA expression of the kinase-encoding gene NUAK2 (SNARK), while NUAK2 expression is abrogated in the presence of IκB-SR.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claim: A feedback loop exists between RELA nuclear translocation and NUAK2 expression.
source: Our identification of a feedback loop between RELA nuclear translocation and NUAK2 expression is analogous to prior findings that NUAK2 increases the activity of the mechanosensitive transcriptional coactivator YAP through stimulation of actin polymerisation and myosin activity (Yuan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on current experimental findings and comparison with previous literature.

claim: NUAK2 increases the activity of the mechanosensitive transcriptional coactivator YAP through stimulation of actin polymerisation and myosin activity.
source: Our identification of a feedback loop between RELA nuclear translocation and NUAK2 expression is analogous to prior findings that NUAK2 increases the activity of the mechanosensitive transcriptional coactivator YAP through stimulation of actin polymerisation and myosin activity (Yuan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2018.

claim: MYPT1 is a substrate for NUAK2.
source: A potential source for further study could consider myosin phosphatase target subunit 1 (MYPT1), a substrate for NUAK2 (Yamamoto et al., 2008) that is reported to mediate NUAK2 regulation of actin stress fibres in growing cells (Vallenius et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yamamoto et al., 2008.

claim: MYPT1 mediates NUAK2 regulation of actin stress fibres in growing cells.
source: A potential source for further study could consider myosin phosphatase target subunit 1 (MYPT1), a substrate for NUAK2 (Yamamoto et al., 2008) that is reported to mediate NUAK2 regulation of actin stress fibres in growing cells (Vallenius et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vallenius et al., 2011.

claim: NUAK2 may be a promising target for potential use in PDAC therapy as kinases contain an ATP-binding cleft that is a druggable pocket.
source: From a therapeutic perspective, NUAK2 may be a promising target to follow-up for potential use in PDAC therapy as kinases contain an ATP-binding cleft that is a druggable pocket and can contain additional druggable sites distal to the ATP or substrate binding pockets conferring inhibitor specificity (Lamba and Ghosh, 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Lamba and Ghosh, 2012.

claim: NUAK2 is a prognostic marker for PDAC and is associated with a favourable prognosis according to The Human Protein Atlas.
source: However, NUAK2 is a prognostic marker for PDAC and is associated with a favourable prognosis according to The Human Protein Atlas, which proposes a potential tumour suppressor role for NUAK2 in PDAC, suggesting that enhancing NUAK2 may be a favourable strategy for PDAC.
evidence: This is based on information from The Human Protein Atlas.

claim: NUAK2 may have a potential tumour suppressor role in PDAC.
source: However, NUAK2 is a prognostic marker for PDAC and is associated with a favourable prognosis according to The Human Protein Atlas, which proposes a potential tumour suppressor role for NUAK2 in PDAC, suggesting that enhancing NUAK2 may be a favourable strategy for PDAC.
evidence: This is speculation based on information from The Human Protein Atlas.

claim: CK666 inhibits the ARP2/3 complex that mediates actin filament nucleation and branching.
source: CK666 inhibits the ARP2/3 complex that mediates actin filament nucleation and branching (Mullins et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mullins et al., 1998.

claim: SMIFH2 inhibits formins.
source: SMIFH2 inhibits formins (Rizvi et al., 2009), which produce long straight filaments by promoting actin nucleation and filament elongation (Pruyne et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rizvi et al., 2009 and Pruyne et al., 2002.

claim: Formins produce long straight filaments by promoting actin nucleation and filament elongation.
source: SMIFH2 inhibits formins (Rizvi et al., 2009), which produce long straight filaments by promoting actin nucleation and filament elongation (Pruyne et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pruyne et al., 2002.

claim: Cytochalasin D binds to the growing end of actin filaments and inhibits polymerisation.
source: Cytochalasin D binds to the growing end of actin filaments and inhibits polymerisation (Schliwa, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schliwa, 1982.

claim: H1152 targets Rho-kinase (ROCK), preventing ROCK phosphorylation of myosin light chain that normally promotes actin-binding and contractility.
source: H1152 targets Rho-kinase (ROCK), preventing ROCK phosphorylation of myosin light chain that normally promotes actin-binding and contractility, while blebbistatin blocks myosin II ATPase and actin contractility (Sasaki et al., 2002; Kovács et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sasaki et al., 2002 and Kovács et al., 2004.

claim: Blebbistatin blocks myosin II ATPase and actin contractility.
source: H1152 targets Rho-kinase (ROCK), preventing ROCK phosphorylation of myosin light chain that normally promotes actin-binding and contractility, while blebbistatin blocks myosin II ATPase and actin contractility (Sasaki et al., 2002; Kovács et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sasaki et al., 2002 and Kovács et al., 2004.

claim: Vinblastine and nocodazole prevent MT assembly.
source: Tubulin-targeting drugs prevent MT assembly (vinblastine and nocodazole), limit MT formation and cause MT depolymerisation (demecolcine), or stabilise MTs and prevent disassembly (paclitaxel) (Spencer and Faulds, 1994; Vasquez et al., 1997; Gigant et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spencer and Faulds, 1994; Vasquez et al., 1997; Gigant et al., 2005.

claim: Demecolcine limits MT formation and causes MT depolymerisation.
source: Tubulin-targeting drugs prevent MT assembly (vinblastine and nocodazole), limit MT formation and cause MT depolymerisation (demecolcine), or stabilise MTs and prevent disassembly (paclitaxel) (Spencer and Faulds, 1994; Vasquez et al., 1997; Gigant et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spencer and Faulds, 1994; Vasquez et al., 1997; Gigant et al., 2005.

claim: Paclitaxel stabilises MTs and prevents disassembly.
source: Tubulin-targeting drugs prevent MT assembly (vinblastine and nocodazole), limit MT formation and cause MT depolymerisation (demecolcine), or stabilise MTs and prevent disassembly (paclitaxel) (Spencer and Faulds, 1994; Vasquez et al., 1997; Gigant et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spencer and Faulds, 1994; Vasquez et al., 1997; Gigant et al., 2005.

claim: Focal adhesion kinase (FAK) regulates turnover of focal adhesions.
source: Focal adhesion kinase (FAK) regulates turnover of focal adhesions, which are integrin-containing complexes linking intracellular actin to extracellular substrates.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FAK function.
